common_name: Lockwood de Forest Rosemary (Cascading Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container starts in spring or fall in full sun and sharply drained soil; this cascading selection is propagated only from cuttings and does not come true from seed.

directions: Lockwood de Forest is a low, spreading rosemary selected from a seedling found in a Santa Barbara garden of the same name, valued for cascading stems that trail 6 to 8 feet while staying under 2 feet tall. The narrow, resinous leaves carry the same high oil content as upright culinary types and can be snipped for cooking, though gardeners most often plant it to spill over raised beds, retaining walls, and large containers. It flowers on and off through fall, winter, and spring with the pale blue blooms typical of the species, drawing early-season pollinators when little else is in bloom. Give it lean, fast-draining soil and full sun; like other trailing rosemaries it declines quickly in heavy or poorly drained ground.

common_name: Roman Beauty Rosemary (Chef's Choice Compact Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; Roman Beauty is propagated from cuttings and is sold under the patented trade name Chef's Choice.

directions: Roman Beauty, marketed under the trademark Chef's Choice, is a compact, slow-growing culinary rosemary selected for a noticeably higher essential-oil content than standard rosemary, giving a spicier, more concentrated flavor from the same amount of leaf. Its dense, finely textured gray-green foliage and pale blue flowers hold a tidy, upright habit that stays under 3 feet, making it a good choice for containers, herb-garden borders, and small kitchen beds where sprawling rosemary cultivars would outgrow the space. Like other culinary rosemaries it thrives on neglect, wanting lean soil, full sun, and minimal supplemental water once established. Harvest sprigs throughout the growing season; the concentrated flavor means a little goes further in cooking than with milder rosemary types.

common_name: Gold Dust Rosemary (Variegated Golden Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Gold Dust is a patented sport of common rosemary and must be propagated vegetatively to keep its variegation true.

directions: Gold Dust is an upright, branching rosemary whose needle-like leaves carry a bright gold edge around a deep green center, giving the whole shrub a variegated glow that holds its color through the growing season better than most golden-leaf herbs. Despite the ornamental foliage it is fully culinary, with the same piney, resinous flavor as green-leaved rosemary, and it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity notably well for a variegated selection. Site it in full sun for the best gold coloration, since shade fades the variegation toward plain green, and give it the same lean, sharply drained soil that all rosemary needs to avoid root and crown rot. Use it as a specimen or low hedge where its color can be appreciated, and harvest sprigs for the kitchen just as you would any culinary rosemary.

common_name: Portuguese Pink Rosemary (Upright Pink-Flowered Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; propagate this cultivar vegetatively, since seed-grown rosemary does not come true to flower color.

directions: Portuguese Pink is an upright culinary rosemary similar in size and habit to Tuscan Blue, but distinguished by soft pink flowers marked with darker pink veining instead of the usual blue-violet. The glossy deep-green foliage is fully aromatic and flavorful, making it as useful in the kitchen as any standard rosemary while adding a less common flower color to the herb border. Its tall, dense growth habit lends itself to hedging, topiary, and use as a specimen shrub, much like other large upright rosemary cultivars. Grow it in full sun with sharp drainage, and prune after flowering to maintain a tight form.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (September-November in zone 9) or very early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Vierling's thick stems and slow-bolting habit let it stand longer before flowering than most dill, extending the fresh-leaf harvest window.

directions: Vierling is a European heirloom dill grown for its steel-blue, finely cut foliage and thick, sturdy stems that hold up well in cut-flower arrangements once the chartreuse seed umbels open. It is notably slow to bolt compared with older dill strains, keeping tender leaf production going longer into warm weather before the plant switches over to flowering and seed. In zone 9, fall sowing lets plants establish through the cool months and reach their full 3-to-5-foot height by spring, when the wide seed heads attract beneficial insects and pollinators. Harvest leaves continuously for fresh dill weed, and let a few plants flower and seed to collect dill seed for pickling or to let the planting self-sow.

planting.note: Direct sow shallowly, barely covering the seed, in late summer to early fall for a fall-through-spring harvest in zone 9, or in very early spring for a quick cool-season crop before heat causes bolting.

directions: Vertissimo is a dense, clump-forming chervil selected for vigor and slow bolting, producing more leaf over a longer harvest window than older curled types before running up to flower. Its dark green, tightly curled foliage regrows quickly after cutting, making it well suited to repeated harvests from the same planting rather than a single cut-and-done crop. Like all chervil it carries a mild anise-parsley flavor best used fresh, since drying or prolonged cooking destroys the delicate flavor. Give it partial shade and consistently moist soil in zone 9, where the cool months from fall through spring are its only realistic growing window.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (September-November in zone 9) for the longest cool-season harvest window, or 2-4 weeks before the last spring frost; Marino resists bolting nearly as well as Santo, giving extra weeks of usable leaf before plants flower.

directions: Marino is an organic cilantro selection bred for slow bolting and a growth habit close to the widely grown Santo strain, but with a slightly spicier, more peppery edge to the leaf flavor than standard cilantro. Plants stay in the leafy stage longer before sending up flower stalks, which stretches the harvest window during the cool months when cilantro grows best in zone 9. Direct sow into the bed rather than transplanting, since the taproot is easily damaged, and succession sow every few weeks through fall and winter for a steady supply. Once plants do bolt, leave a few to flower and set seed, which can be harvested and used whole or ground as coriander spice.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for zone 9's main cilantro season, or 2-4 weeks before the last spring frost; Jantar bolts noticeably later than older standard cilantro strains, giving roughly an extra week to ten days of usable leaf in university trial comparisons.

directions: Jantar is a Central European coriander cultivar bred for a longer productive leaf stage before bolting, developed for both fresh cilantro leaf and coriander seed production. In side-by-side trials it has held its leafy stage notably longer than common cilantro strains, giving growers extra harvest time from the same planting before plants run to flower. Its aromatic seed also has a good oil yield, so gardeners who let a planting go to seed get a worthwhile coriander spice harvest in addition to the fresh leaf crop. Grow it exactly as you would other cilantro: direct-sown, in full sun, kept evenly moist, and sown in fall or very early spring to avoid the heat that triggers bolting in zone 9.
